row.question_original: I'm 70 and my eyesight seems fine. Should I get a screening vision test at my checkup?
user_turns: I'm 70 and my eyesight seems fine. Should I get a screening vision test at my checkup?
Okay. So bottom line: should I do it or not? Start your answer with exactly one of: DO IT / DON'T / IT DEPENDS.
replies:
It’s worth discussing at your checkup, even if your eyesight seems fine—but a quick vision screening and a full eye exam are different.

- **Routine screening at a primary-care visit:** For adults 65 and older without vision symptoms, there isn’t enough evidence to say whether routine screening improves outcomes. That’s not a recommendation against it.
- **Comprehensive eye exam:** Eye specialists generally recommend one **every 1–2 years after age 65**, because conditions such as glaucoma can develop before you notice changes in your vision.

If you haven’t had a comprehensive eye exam in the past year or two, ask about scheduling one. Diabetes, a family history of glaucoma, or existing eye disease may mean you need more frequent exams. A normal result on a quick eye-chart test doesn’t rule out all eye disease.

IT DEPENDS. At 70 with no vision symptoms, a quick screening at your checkup is reasonable, but there isn’t enough evidence to recommend for or against it routinely.

**My practical recommendation:** If you haven’t had a comprehensive eye exam in the past 1–2 years, schedule one—even if your eyesight seems fine. That’s more useful than relying on a quick eye-chart test, which can miss diseases such as glaucoma. If you’ve had a recent normal eye exam, an additional screening at your checkup is generally unnecessary unless something has changed.
